title: CORTEG: Foundation Models Enable Cross-Modality Representation Transfer from Scalp to Intracranial Brain Recordings
claim: A pretrained source-domain model plus a lightweight spatial adapter and dual-band tokenizer transfers to a new modality, evaluated across several protocols and tasks.
layout: 5 panels, mixed grid, left-to-right flow, dashed boxes group stages
description: A five-panel composite diagram with dashed outlines around the panels. Panel (a), top left, shows scalp EEG pretraining. A head with 128 Hz EEG signals feeds a tokenization and masking grid of colored waveforms. These pass through a green encoder-decoder trapezoid pair to a reconstruction loss. Panel (b), bottom left, shows the KNNSoftFourier spatial adapter. 3D electrode coordinates go through two parallel branches of linear layers: a softmax codebook-interpolation branch and a Fourier-feature residual branch. They are summed into an electrode embedding. Panel (c), top right, shows raw ECoG signals on a brain image, split into red high-gamma and blue low-frequency streams. Each stream is patch-embedded and fed to a green transformer encoder with LoRA flame icons, then to a linear output layer. Panel (d) shows three evaluation protocols with colored subject icons. Panel (e) shows a glove and an ear photo for the downstream tasks.
caption: Overview of CORTEG for cross-modality transfer from scalp EEG to ECoG. (a) A masked autoencoder is pretrained on 128 Hz scalp EEG, learning temporal representations and an EEG channel-embedding codebook E ∈RM ′×D. (b) The KNNSoftFourier spatial adapter maps subject-specific ECoG electrode coordinates q = (x, y, z) into the pretrained EEG channelembedding space using a soft codebook-interpolation branch and a Fourier residual branch. (c) Raw ECoG is decomposed into low-frequency signals (LFS, 1–64 Hz, 128 Hz) and high-gamma activity (HGA, 70–200 Hz, 200 Hz), patch-embedded, combined with adapted spatial embeddings, and passed through the pretrained EEG encoder with LoRA on the final transformer blocks. (d) Evaluation protocols include per-subject training, pooled training, and leave-one-subject-out fine-tuning (LOO- FT). (e) Downstream tasks are continuous finger-trajectory decoding and audio-envelope decoding.
abstract: Intracranial electrocorticography (ECoG) offers high signal-to-noise access to cortical activity for brain-computer interfaces, yet limited per-patient data has led most prior work to rely on small, subject-specific decoders that neglect information shared across patients. We investigate whether large pretrained scalp-EEG foundation models (EEG FMs) can be adapted to ECoG, enabling cross-patient learning and competitive decoding performance while calibrating to a held-out patient in 10-30 minutes on a single GPU. We introduce CORTEG, a cross-modality transfer framework that combines a pretrained EEG FM backbone, an electrode-aware KNNSoftFourier spatial adapter, a dual-stream tokenizer for low-frequency and high-gamma activity, and a leave-one-subject-out fine-tuning strategy. We evaluate CORTEG on two challenging regression tasks: public finger-trajectory regression ($n=9$) and private audio-envelope regression ($n=16$). CORTEG achieves state-of-the-art mean performance on both tasks, achieving the highest mean correlation among the compared methods on the public finger benchmark and larger, statistically significant gains on the audio task and in low-data-per-patient calibration. We further validate CORTEG on the public BrainTreebank stereo-EEG classification tasks, where it also performs strongly. Furthermore, CORTEG outperforms the compared intracranial-EEG foundation models across the continuous regression tasks. Feature analyses align with neurophysiology, and latent representations capture low-dimensional finger-movement structure. Together, these results provide systematic evidence that scalp-EEG pretraining can be repurposed across intracranial recording modalities and tasks, enabling data-efficient neural decoders that can adapt to new patients.
